title: From Grazing to Growing Up: Matching Mathematical Tools to Ecological Complexity

annotations.one_line_context: This talk explains how applied mathematicians collaborate with biologists to build differential equation models that capture multi-scale ecological dynamics and population oscillations.

abstract: Classical population models often rely on simple, unstructured differential equations that assume uniform life stages and instantaneous growth. In reality, species have stage-specific traits and behavioral adaptations that require more complicated mathematical tools. In this talk, I will illustrate how applied mathematicians collaborate with biologists to build mechanistic, first-principles models that capture multi-scale ecological dynamics. We begin with grazing, introducing co-limitation functions to capture how nutrient limitations alter feeding behavior. We then transition to growing up, using stage-structured and delay differential equations to model how high nutrient demands in juveniles create developmental bottlenecks. We demonstrate how stage-specific nutrient demands shift stability boundaries and control population oscillations under enrichment. Ultimately, we show how matching the right mathematical framework to biological reality uncovers novel dynamical behaviors and yields deeper insights into complex ecological systems.

title: On-the-Fly Reduced-Order Modeling via Matrix and Tensor Network Low-Rank Approximations

annotations.one_line_context: This talk discusses computational strategies and low-rank approximation methods for solving high-dimensional matrix and tensor differential equations directly in adaptive forms.

abstract: Some of the most computationally demanding problems in science and engineering involve large-scale and high-dimensional matrix and tensor differential equations (MDEs and TDEs). These arise in applications ranging from the Schrodinger equation and kinetic transport models (Fokker-Planck and Boltzmann equations) to probability density function transport in turbulent combustion and Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations. Even in three-dimensional settings, such as turbulent reacting flows, the sheer scale and multiscale structure of the dynamics render direct numerical treatment prohibitively expensive. The underlying challenge is structural: the number of degrees of freedom grows combinatorially with dimension, resolution, or parametric complexity. Low-rank matrix and their extension to tensor network approximations provide a principled framework to address this challenge by exploiting intrinsic low-dimensional structure and multi-dimensional correlations in the solution. In this presentation, we focus on computational strategies for solving nonlinear MDEs and TDEs directly in adaptive low-rank form. We introduce a novel formulation based on adaptive cross interpolation and develop CUR-type decompositions grounded in the Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (DEIM) for matrix, tensor-train, and Tucker representations. These DEIM-CUR algorithms enable on-the-fly reduced-order modeling with near-optimal accuracy for broad classes of nonlinear dynamical systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these approaches across applications in turbulent combustion, sensitivity analysis, uncertainty quantification, and both high-dimensional and large-scale partial differential equations.

title: Cut, Paste, Blow Up: a Grothendieck Ring for Varieties with Boundary

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces a logarithmic Grothendieck ring of varieties with boundary and explores its motivic invariants.

abstract: How many solutions does xy = 1 have over a field with q elements? The answer, q - 1, depends on q; the recipe behind it does not. The Grothendieck ring of varieties records exactly these recipes: cut a variety into pieces, multiply independent choices, and write down a formal class class [X] that contains point-counts over every finite field as well as Hodge-theoretic and birational information over C. What if varieties come with a boundary? Invariance under choice of boundary forces w(w + L - 1) = 0: the boundary appears as a "negative torus." In joint work with A. Gross, D. Holmes, P. Spelier and J. Vogel, we show this single relation is the whole story: the logarithmic Grothendieck ring of varieties with boundary is K_0(Var)[w]/w(w+L-1). I will develop this from explicit counts on planes, blowups and marked projective lines, with no logarithmic geometry assumed, and end with a surprise: the naive logarithmic Hodge table fails the scissors test, while its alternating specialization survives as a genuine logarithmic motivic invariant.

title: Algebraic structures and logarithmic geometry

annotations.one_line_context: This talk explains how geometric structures can be viewed as monad algebras, with applications to logarithmic geometry and functorial tropicalization.

abstract:
(Joint with Peter Haine) Many geometric structures can be described as 

emephal

 algebras for a suitable monad. E.g., compact Hausdorff spaces are exactly the algebras for the ultrafilter monad on sets.  I will explain this point of view through several concrete examples, starting with free abelian groups and rings, and then discussing ultrafilters, Eilenberg--Moore categories, and Kleisli categories. The emphasis will be on examples rather than category theory.  The main application is in logarithmic geometry. I will explain how logarithmic maps can be realized as Kleisli morphisms for a natural monad built from Olsson's logarithmic stack. This leads to a functorial tropicalization construction for logarithmic schemes, recovering the usual fans of toric varieties and toroidal embeddings while remaining functorial for arbitrary logarithmic maps. (This talk is meant to be accessible to graduate students)

title: Brill--Noether theory of curves on K3 surfaces

annotations.one_line_context: This talk surveys recent results on the refined Brill-Noether theory of curves on K3 surfaces and its relation to unstable vector bundles.

abstract: Brill--Noether theory studies linear systems on an algebraic curve. K3 surfaces have been central in Brill--Noether theory since Lazarfeld's proof of the Brill--Noether theorem, which describes the linear series on a general curve of genus $g$. In this talk, we'll survey some recent results concerning the Brill--Noether theory of curves on K3 surfaces. Specifically, we'll discuss a refined Brill--Noether theory, which aims to understand the linear series on curves with a given Brill--Noether special linear series, and related unstable vector bundles on K3 surfaces with applications to the dimensions of components of Giesker--Petri loci in $\mathcal{M}_g$, parameterizing curves admitting a linear series with non-injective Petri map.

title: Moduli spaces and heights on stacks

annotations.one_line_context: This talk presents a moduli-theoretic approach to heights on stacks over function fields to study arithmetic counting problems.

abstract: Many counting problems in arithmetic statistics can be formulated as counting points of bounded height on moduli stacks over global fields. Ellenberg, Satriano, and Zureick-Brown introduced a theory of heights on stacks that provides a common framework for studying these problems. In this talk, I will present a moduli-theoretic approach to heights on stacks over function fields, inspired by Abramovich and Vistoli’s theory of twisted stable maps. The idea is to construct moduli spaces parametrizing points of fixed height, translating arithmetic counting problems into questions about the geometry of these spaces. I will describe this construction for a suitable class of stacks and outline an approach to more general stacks that is closely related to the geometry of the moduli space of vector bundles on a curve. This is based on joint work with Park and Satriano.

title: Geometric Tevelev degrees of projective space

annotations.one_line_context: This talk explains a complete calculation of geometric Tevelev degrees of projective space using Schubert calculus and torus orbit closures.

abstract: The geometric Tevelev degrees of projective space enumerate general, pointed curves with fixed complex structure interpolating through the maximal number of points in P^r. The study of the corresponding virtual invariants goes back to the beginning of Gromov-Witten theory in the 1990s, whereas the closely related problem of enumerating linear series on general curves goes back even earlier, to the 19th century. We explain a complete calculation of the geometric Tevelev degrees of projective space in terms of Schubert calculus, which interpolates between both of these worlds. The final answer involves torus orbit closures on Grassmannians, which are fundamental objects in matroid theory. Recent work with Saskia Solotko expresses the invariants alternatively in terms of combinatorics of words, via the RSK correspondence.

title: Continuous-space occupancy models

annotations.one_line_context: This talk presents a new class of spatial occupancy models using a clipped Gaussian process to infer species distributions in continuous space.

abstract: Occupancy models are commonly used to infer species distributions over large spatial extents while accounting for imperfect detection. Current approaches, however, are unable to model species occurrence over continuous spatial domains while accounting for the discrete spatial domain of the observed data. We develop a new class of spatial occupancy models that embeds a change of spatial support between the observed data and occurrence process. We use a clipped Gaussian process to represent species occurrence in continuous space which can provide inferences at a finer resolution than the observed occupancy data. Our approach is beneficial because it allows for more realistic models of species occurrence, can account for species occurring in only a portion of a surveyed site, and can relate detection probabilities to these within-site occurrence proportions. We show how our model can be fit using Bayesian methods and develop a computationally efficient MCMC algorithm. We also show how our framework can be extended to handle multiple years of data to learn about species occupancy dynamics in continuous space. We demonstrate our model using simulated data and compare our approach to alternative spatial occupancy models. We also use our model to analyze ovenbird occurrence data collected in New Hampshire, USA.

title: Understanding CNN Efficiency: Statistical Generative Models for Unstructured Image Data

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces novel statistical generative models to analyze the efficiency and approximation capabilities of Convolutional Neural Networks in image analysis.

abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are foundational in modern image analysis due to their ability to efficiently learn feature representations. However, theoretical understanding of their efficiency remains limited, largely due to inadequate modeling of image structures and their interaction with CNNs. To address this, we introduce novel statistical generative models (SGMs) that decompose images into task-relevant signals and noise, capturing the complexities of natural image data. Based on these SGMs, we propose a feature mapping approach (FMA) to characterize the transformation from raw image data to feature vectors. We analyze CNNs' approximation capabilities, their adaptation to low-dimensional structures, and their efficiency in vision tasks, ultimately developing statistical learning theories for CNN-based image analysis. Our findings reveal the challenges inherent in vision tasks and highlight CNNs' remarkable efficiency in addressing them, providing new insights into their theoretical and practical capabilities. This is based on the joint work with Dr. Guohao Shen.

title: ML/AI-accelerated autonomous experimentation with digital twins: a statistician's playground

annotations.one_line_context: This talk explores how machine learning and AI can accelerate autonomous scientific experimentation using digital twin simulators.

abstract: An emerging use of ML/AI in science is autonomous scientific experimentation, which has shown promise for self-driving laboratories in, e.g., material and biotech engineering. This automation is fueled by the rise of "digital twin" simulators that enable reliable virtual experimentation of complex physical systems. One bottleneck, however, is the time-intensive nature of virtual experiments, which can take thousands of CPU hours to perform on a supercomputer. In this talk, we explore several ways that ML/AI can accelerate autonomous experimentation for timely scientific decision-making. The first is the use of physics-informed ML/AI models that incorporate known physics, e.g., boundary information, to enhance model learning from experimental data. The second is the use of ML/AI-enhanced optimization solvers to effectively design experimental runs for complex high-dimensional systems. Time permitting, the third is the use of robust transfer learning models that effectively transfer information from existing literature (e.g., extracted via large language models) to guide experimentation. We explore the effectiveness of these approaches in ongoing scientific collaborations.

title: Statistical Foundations of Deep Learning: Toward Efficient and Trustworthy AI

annotations.one_line_context: This talk presents a statistical perspective on deep learning, highlighting Bayesian neural networks and theoretical validation for trustworthy AI.

abstract: Deep learning has transformed modern artificial intelligence through increasingly flexible models, large datasets, and scalable computation. For statisticians, however, its rapid development raises fundamental questions about statistical modeling, inference, theory, and computational efficiency. In this talk, we present a statistical perspective on deep learning, focusing on Bayesian neural networks, variational inference, theoretical validation, and structurally sparse deep networks. We discuss how statistical modeling and optimization can provide theoretical guarantees, quantify approximation effects, and produce more efficient deep-learning models without substantial loss of predictive performance. Applications to high-dimensional and complex data illustrate the role of statistical methodology in developing reliable and computationally efficient AI. More broadly, the talk explores how statistical theory, machine learning, and optimization can work together to build more principled and trustworthy AI.

title: Early-stopped aggregation: Adaptive inference with computational efficiency

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces early-stopped aggregation, a novel framework for efficient model aggregation in Bayesian and frequentist settings.

abstract: When considering a model selection or, more generally, an aggregation approach for adaptive statistical inference, it is often necessary to compute estimators over a wide range of model complexities including unnecessarily large models even when the true data-generating process is relatively simple, due to the lack of prior knowledge. This requirement can lead to substantial computational inefficiency. In this work, we propose a novel framework for efficient model aggregation called the early-stopped aggregation (ESA): instead of computing and aggregating estimators for all candidate models, we compute only a small number of simpler ones using an early-stopping criterion and aggregate only these for final inference. Our framework is versatile and applies to both Bayesian model selection, in particular, within the variational Bayes framework, and frequentist estimation, including a general penalized estimation setting. We investigate adaptive optimal property of the ESA approach across three learning paradigms. We first show that ESA achieves optimal adaptive contraction rates in the variational Bayes setting under mild conditions. We extend this result to variational empirical Bayes, where prior hyperparameters are chosen in a data-dependent manner. In addition, we apply the ESA approach to frequentist aggregation including both penalization-based and sample-splitting implementations, and establish corresponding theory. As we demonstrate, there is a clear unification between early-stopped Bayes and frequentist penalized aggregation, with a common "energy" functional comprising a data-fitting term and a complexity-control term that drives both procedures. We further present several applications and numerical studies that highlight the efficiency and strong performance of the proposed approach.

title: Generalized Rothe diagrams for orthogonal roots

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces a root-theoretic framework using orthogonal roots and generalized Rothe diagrams that generalizes various combinatorial and algebraic structures.

abstract:
Let \(\Phi\) be a simply-laced root system with Weyl group \(W\), let \(U\) be a set of positive roots in \(\Phi\), and let \(\Omega_U\) be the set of all maximum-cardinality orthogonal subsets of \(U\). Define the generalized Rothe diagram of each \(R\in \Omega_U\) to be the set
\[ D_U(R)=\{\alpha\in U : s__\beta(\alpha)>0 \text{ for all } \beta\in R\}. \]
We show how the set \(\Omega_U\) and the diagrams \(D_U(R)\) provide a root-theoretic framework that recovers many widely studied algebraic and combinatorial objects. For example, for a suitable choice of \(U\) in type \(D_{2k}\), the set \(\Omega_U\) can be identified with the symmetric group \(S_k\), and the diagrams \(D_U(R)\) coincide with the traditional Rothe diagrams of permutations. For another choice in type \(D_{2k}\), the elements of \(\Omega_U\) can be identified with the fixed-point-free involutions in \(S_{2k}\), and the diagrams \(D_U(R)\) recover the involution Rothe diagrams used by Hamaker–Marberg–Pawlowski to obtain their involution Schubert polynomials. Our other examples involve perfect matchings, rook configurations, labelled Fano planes, del Pezzo surfaces, and minuscule representations. The set \(\Omega_U\) also forms a quasiparabolic set in the sense of Rains–Vazirani in all our examples, which endows \(\Omega_U\) with a Bruhat-like partial order and natural connections to the Iwahori–Hecke algebra of \(W\). (Joint work with Richard Green.)
speaker: Tianyuan Xu

title: Zeta functions of modular curves and abstract isogeny graphs

annotations.one_line_context: The speaker discusses abstract isogeny graphs and their zeta functions, relating them to modular curves over finite fields.

abstract: Isogeny graphs of supersingular elliptic curves have broad application, from the study and computation of modular forms to post-quantum cryptography. This is in part because the family of q-isogeny graphs in characteristic p (with prime p varying, for a fixed prime q) is Ramanujan. One tool for studying a graph is its Ihara zeta function, defined as an Euler product over the primes of the graph. Defining the zeta function formally requires a graph in the sense of Serre and Bass, i.e. a directed graph equipped with a fixed-point free involution on the edge set. In general, isogeny graphs fail to be graphs in this sense. In this talk, I will discuss joint work with Lau, Orvis, Scullard, and Zobernig in which we introduce abstract isogeny graphs along with their zeta functions; these graphs capture the combinatorial structure of supersingular isogeny graphs (with level structure). I will survey some of our results, including an analogue of Ihara’s determinant formula, showing in particular that the zeta function is rational. We use this formula and the Eichler-Shimura relation to give a formula relating the zeta function of a q-isogeny graph with level-H structure (for certain H, including B0(N) and B1(N)) to the Hasse-Weil zeta functions of two associated modular curves over the finite field Fq, generalizing results of Hashimoto, Sugiyama, and Lei-Muller.

title: Arithmetic on Markoff surfaces

annotations.one_line_context: This talk explores the Markoff group action on solutions to the Markoff equation and presents new techniques to address related conjectures.

abstract: In this talk, we study the Markoff group action on solutions to the Markoff equation and its impact on questions in number theory and combinatorial group theory. The orbit structure of this action is predicted to be trivial outside of a few known exceptions by conjectures of Baragar, Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, and McCullough–Wanderley, which have been verified in some case by work of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, Chen, and just recently, Kingsbury-Neuschotz. We will present alternative techniques that establish these conjectures in additional settings.

title: Applications of kernel methods in data-driven reduced-order models

annotations.one_line_context: This talk explores how kernel methods can improve data-driven reduced-order models for computationally expensive simulations.

abstract: Many-query simulation tasks like computational design and uncertainty quantification require repeated evaluations of high-fidelity numerical models. However, the computational cost and runtime of a single high-fidelity simulation can make many-query tasks computationally infeasible. In these scenarios, it is desirable to substitute the high-fidelity model with a computationally efficient surrogate to drastically decrease the computational costs of many-query tasks with minimal accuracy loss. This presentation details recent advancements in non-intrusive reduced-order modeling, a data-driven surrogate modeling paradigm, leveraging tools from kernel methods. Kernel methods provide a means for data-driven function approximation that requires minimal training cost, enables the enforcement of desired structural properties (e.g., smoothness, polynomial structure, closure terms), has robust mathematical foundations, and admits rigorous error estimates. We apply kernel methods in two key components of a reduced-order model (ROM): 1) nonlinear dimension reduction and 2) identification of ROM dynamics in the latent space. In the first part of the talk, we present kernel-based nonlinear manifolds, which generalizes recent work on quadratic manifolds (QMs). This class of approaches augments POD with a nonlinear correction term in the reconstruction map, which we learn via kernel methods. We compare our approach to POD and several recent QM approaches on data from several example problems, including a 2D boundary layer problem and a 3D solid mechanics problem. In the second part of the talk, we present kernel ROMs, a non-intrusive ROM approach also relying on kernel methods. While existing approaches approximate ROM dynamics by learning low-dimensional matrix operators, our approach approximates ROM dynamics using kernel methods. We show that our approach can produce interpretable ROMs whose structure mirrors full-order model structure by embedding judiciously chosen feature maps into the kernel and admits a computable a posteriori error estimate. The approach is demonstrated in several numerical experiments that include comparisons to operator inference.

title: Efficient Solution of Sequences of Parametrized Lyapunov Equations With Applications

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces two novel numerical procedures to efficiently solve sequences of parametrized Lyapunov equations.

abstract: Sequences of parametrized Lyapunov equations arise in many application settings. Moreover, the solutions of these equations are often intermediate steps in an overall procedure whose main goal is to compute the trace of a matrix that solves a structured Lyapunov equation. We are interested in addressing problems where the parameter dependency of the coefficient matrix is encoded as a low-rank modification to a seed, fixed matrix. We propose two novel numerical procedures that fully exploit such a common structure. The first one builds upon the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury (SMW) formula and recycling Krylov techniques, and it is well-suited for small dimensional problems as it makes use of dense numerical linear algebra tools. The second algorithm can instead address large-scale problems by relying on state-of-the-art projection techniques based on the extended Krylov subspace. We test the new algorithms on several problems arising in the study of damped vibrational systems and the analyses of output synchronization problems for multi-agent systems. Our results show that the algorithms we propose are superior to state-of-the-art techniques as they are able to remarkably speed up the computation of accurate solutions.

annotations.one_line_context: This talk discusses an Anderson accelerated preconditioned splitting method for solving complex-symmetric linear systems.

abstract: We will talk about the design and development of an Anderson Accelerated Preconditioned Modified Hermitian and Skew-Hermitian Splitting (AA-PMHSS) method for solving complex-symmetric linear systems with application to electromagnetics problems, such as wave scattering and eddy currents. While it has been shown that the Anderson acceleration of real linear systems is essentially equivalent to GMRES, we show here that the formulation using Anderson acceleration leads to a more performant method. We show that the method can be generalised to many matrix splittings enabling a method that can be seen as a inexactly left-preconditioned GMRES.
speaker: Måns Andersson

title: Enhancing the adaptive Antoulas-Anderson algorithm with iteratively reweighted least squares

annotations.one_line_context: This talk presents refinements to the Antoulas-Anderson algorithm to construct rational approximations of minimal degree.

abstract: Given a set of data on an interval, the adaptive Antoulas-Anderson (AAA) algorithm is a widely used method to efficiently construct highly accurate rational approximations to the data. Broadly, AAA fits the given data adaptively by interpolating a subset of the data and fitting the remaining data via a relaxed (linearized) rational least-squares fit. While AAA can often produce rational approximations accurate to any prescribed tolerance, these approximations may have degrees larger than what is actually required to meet the given tolerance. In this work, we consider the adaptive construction of interpolating rational approximations while aiming for the smallest feasible degree to satisfy a given error tolerance. To this end, we introduce refinement approaches to the linear least-squares step of the classical AAA algorithm that aim to minimize the true rational least-squares error with respect to the given data. Furthermore, we theoretically analyze the derived approaches in terms of the corresponding gradients from the resulting minimization problems and use these insights to propose a new greedy framework that ensures monotonic error convergence. Numerical examples from function approximation and model order reduction verify the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm to construct accurate rational approximations of small degrees.
speaker: Mike Ackermann

title: Parameter Recovery via Continuous Data Assimilation for the steady Navier Stokes Equations

annotations.one_line_context: This talk explores using continuous data assimilation for parameter identification in the steady Navier-Stokes equations.

abstract: Recent advances in equation discovery methods such as SINDy have highlighted the growing interest in identifying governing parameters and models directly from data. In this work, we take a complementary approach grounded in analysis and numerical PDE methods: we recover unknown physical parameters via continuous data assimilation (CDA). We study the steady incompressible Navier–Stokes equations with "unknown" viscosity and assume access only to partial velocity observations. By combining CDA with nonlinear solvers (e.g. Picard, Picard–Newton iteration), we show that the assimilation error scales linearly with the viscosity mismatch. This linear relationship leads to a simple and efficient parameter recovery algorithm based on a small number of CDA solves. Our analysis establishes well-posedness and convergence of the CDA system with inconsistent viscosity, as well as quadratic convergence of the CDA–Picard–Newton iteration. Numerical experiments for 3D driven cavity flows at moderate to high Reynolds numbers demonstrate rapid and high-accuracy recovery of the viscosity. The results illustrate how data assimilation can serve not only for state reconstruction, but also as a practical and mathematically grounded tool for parameter identification in nonlinear fluid models.
speaker: Jorge Reyes

title: An Efficient Low-Rank Solver for Nonlinear Convection–Diffusion Equations

annotations.one_line_context: This talk presents a novel low-rank solver for nonlinear convection-diffusion equations based on the explicit-implicit-null method.

abstract: Convection-diffusion equations arise in a wide range of scientific and engineering applications, including fluid transport, heat conduction, and the evolution of passive scalars. In many practical settings, especially in diffusion-dominated regimes, the solution often exhibits a low-rank structure. The structure has motivated the development of low-rank methods, which have shown success to solving linear convection-diffusion equations but fewer work has been done to the nonlinear diffusion case. In this work, We present a novel low rank method which can handle these nonlinear diffusion efficiently. The approach is based on the explicit-implicit-null (EIN) method, where a linear and easy invertible stiff term is added and then subtracted. The stability restriction related to explicit schemes is then relaxed and nonlinear solver required by fully implicit schemes is avoided simultaneously. The low-rank solver is based on the cross approximation, which uses CrossDEIM algorithms for nonlinear term evaluation. Finally, we show the effectiveness of the solver for a few test cases.
speaker: Hengyi Shi

title: What to Interpolate for L2 Optimal Approximation

annotations.one_line_context: This talk revisits the L2 optimal approximation problem, highlighting Hermite interpolation as a necessary condition for optimality.

abstract: In this talk, we revisit the L2 optimal approximation problem through various formulations and applications, exploring its rich mathematical structure and diverse implications. We begin with the classical case where the optimal approximant is a rational function, highlighting how Hermite interpolation at specific reflected points emerges as the necessary condition for optimality. Building on this foundation, we consider extensions that introduce additional structure to rational approximations and relax certain restrictions, revealing new dimensions of the problem. Throughout, we demonstrate how Hermite interpolation at reflected points serves as a unifying theme across different domains and applications.
speaker: Serkan Gugercin

title: Generalized Method of Lines: New Runge-Kutta Methods for Hyperbolic Conservation Laws

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces a generalized method of lines that allows different spatial operators within multi-stage Runge-Kutta time steps.

abstract: The conventional method-of-lines framework for time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) relies on method of lines: when using a multi-stage Runge-Kutta (RK) method for time integration, the exact same spatial operator is evaluated at every stage. In this talk, we challenge this default assumption and introduce a generalized method of lines for hyperbolic conservation laws. By allowing different spatial operators to be used at different RK stages, we open up a new design space for numerical schemes. We present novel RK methods that hybridize distinct Discontinuous Galerkin (DG) spatial discretizations within a single time step. We will discuss the theoretical formulation of these multi-operator schemes, explore various hybridization strategies, and highlight their specific advantages in terms of stability, accuracy, and efficiency.
speaker: Qifan Chen

title: On Minimax Optimal Transport and Differential Games

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces a minimax formulation of optimal transport linking static transport problems to differential games.

abstract: This talk is on a modification of the optimal transport (OT) problem. We introduce a novel minimax formulation of the quadratic (OT) problem, generalizing the classical Monge and Kantorovich frameworks. We define a Nash Equilibrium Transport Plan (NETP) as a solution to a zero-sum game between two teams, where the cost function depends on pairs of paths. The teams’ strategies are transport plans over path spaces connecting given source and target measures. We establish conditions for the existence and uniqueness of NETPs, leveraging compactness and semi-continuity arguments. This path-space formulation allows us to incorporate interaction terms, such as pursuit-evasion dynamics, connecting our static problem to differential games. Furthermore, we explore duality and characterizations of the Nash-Monge-Kantorovich transport map. We conclude this talk with a discussion on strategies and associated challenges for numerically solving these problems. This is a work in progress which may provide a foundation for analyzing competitive transport phenomena with applications in multi-agent systems and game theory.
speaker: Edward Huynh

title: Completely-Positive and Trace Preserving Schemes for the Lindblad Equation using Tensor Train Compression

annotations.one_line_context: This talk proposes low-rank, completely positive and trace preserving schemes for simulating open quantum systems using tensor trains.

abstract: We propose a family of low-rank, completely positive and trace preserving (CPTP) schemes for the Lindblad equation, a common model for open quantum systems. Low-rank representation is employed at two levels: the density matrix is factorized into the product of tall-skinny matrices, and the columns of these matrices are further compressed using the tensor train (TT) format, also know as matrix product states (MPS). This representation fits naturally into our recent Kraus is King scheme for the Lindblad equation, whose underlying operations are arithmetic on the columns of the low-rank factor matrices. We show how these operations can be performed efficiently in the TT/MPS format, with particular emphasis on the primary bottleneck: density matrix rank-truncation. We perform extensive numerical experiments demonstrating the convergence of this scheme and its efficiency in simulating open quantum systems with millions of degrees of freedom using only modest computational resources.
speaker: Peter DelMastro

title: Preconditioner updating for high-order DG FEM systems using Sparse Approximate Mappings from L-1 constrained sparsity pattern generator.

annotations.one_line_context: This talk presents a modified sparse approximate mapping algorithm using the lasso problem for efficient preconditioner updating in high-order DG FEM systems.

abstract: Preconditioning of high-order discrete Galerkin (DG) systems presents a challenge in applications such as topology optimization and PDE-based inverse problems. Computing an accurate preconditioner for the linear system in each step can make the solve process a computational bottleneck. The sequence of linear systems to solve can be similar enough to warrant a cheap preconditioner updating scheme. The sparse approximate mapping (SAM) is one such method that was introduced in Preconditioning Parametrizing Linear Systems by Carr et al. Each column of the SAM is solved from a least-squares problem. The method is cheap as long as the underlying sparsity pattern is sufficiently sparse. However, as revealed in prior research, there is no intuitive choice for such a pattern. In this talk, we present a modification of the existing SAM computation algorithm that solves the lasso problem instead. We use the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm to solve the lasso problem for each column. We demonstrate that the parameters of ADMM and the regularization parameter can be heuristically selected to compute patterns for SAMs that are significantly sparse.
speaker: Achintya Sunil

title: Randomization methods for big-data

annotations.one_line_context: This talk discusses randomization methods applied to big data problems.

speaker: Stephen Becker

title: Multi-Agent Online Learning under Heterogeneity and Temporal Variations

annotations.one_line_context: This talk presents multi-agent online learning frameworks for clustered personalized federated learning and distributed image reconstruction using ADMM.

abstract: Multi-agent online learning has emerged as a powerful framework for addressing large-scale problems with temporal variation and system heterogeneity. This talk presents two research efforts that apply these ideas in distinct settings. The first work studies clustered personalized federated learning under heterogeneous data distributions through a repeated multi-agent learning framework. Instead of enforcing static cluster assignments, we model personalization as a dynamic decision process and analyze its stability using no-regret learning dynamics. This perspective leads to stable grouping behavior and improved learning performance under evolving system conditions. In the second work, we study distributed reconstruction of a collection of images using an online ADMM framework in which consensus penalties are adapted over time rather than fixed, addressing limitations of static methods in handling spatial heterogeneity and partial observability. The ADMM iterations are interpreted as a dynamical system, with penalty weights acting as control variables updated via partial feedback to enable data-aware, pixel-level consensus. This online control formulation achieves near-optimal performance via dynamic regret guarantees while preserving convergence of weighted inexact ADMM.
speaker: Priyanka Sinha

title: Convergence Analysis for Infinite GMRES

annotations.one_line_context: This talk discusses preliminary convergence results based on the numerical range for the Infinite GMRES algorithm.

abstract: Many applications require the solution of large-scale linear systems that have nonlinear parameter dependence. The Infinite GMRES algorithm, developed by Jarlebring and Correnty in 2022, converts these finite-dimensional systems into infinite-dimensional systems with linear parameter dependence. This transformation involves a linearization process that results in a system with a special companion-like structure. Due to the shift-invariance property of Krylov subspaces, all choices of parameter give the same Krylov subspaces. Thus performing the Arnoldi process for one parameter enables the efficient construction of the GMRES iterates for all parameter values. The special structure of the right-hand-side vector of the infinite-dimensional system allows this Arnoldi process to be executed with finite-dimensional vectors, where the dimension grows with every iteration. As such, Infinite GMRES uses finite-length Krylov basis vectors to solve an infinite-dimensional system. The special structure of the infinite-dimensional system invites further investigation into the convergence behavior of the Infinite GMRES residual norm. We aim to understand how various components of this system, including the size and nature of the block matrices, the number of blocks, and the choice of parameter value influence convergence behavior. In this presentation, we will discuss preliminary convergence results based on the numerical range.
speaker: Jordan Jackson

title: Dynamically Updating Preconditioners with Solver Information

annotations.one_line_context: This talk discusses simple strategies to dynamically update preconditioners using information derived during the solve.

abstract: Preconditioners are essential for fast convergence of iterative linear solvers, but the computation of a good preconditioner can be quite expensive (for example, algebraic multigrid (AMG) preconditioners). In some cases, such as matrix-free solvers, computing a preconditioner is even more complicated, and some cheap and effective preconditioners cannot be used as the matrix is not available. This cost is even worse in simulations where the system matrix changes every timestep, nonlinear step, or optimization step (in PDE-constrained optimization). Even if we can compute a good preconditioner, we often still see some convergence issues due to various complicating factors, PDE coefficients that vary drastically in space or due to strong nonlinearity, highly deformed meshes, and poor meshes due to geometric complexity. On the other hand, if we solve the same system many times (time-stepping with a fixed time step) or the system changes slowly, we have substantial opportunity to learn properties of the system from these solves and we can dynamically update the preconditioner or learn a better preconditioner. I will discuss simple strategies to update the preconditioner dynamically using information that is derived during the solve and provide methods for analysis.
speaker: Eric de Sturler

title: A fast scheme for the Boltzmann equation based on low-rank approximation

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces a fast numerical scheme for the Boltzmann equation using tensor train low-rank approximation.

abstract: The Boltzmann equation can be lifted to a higher-dimensional linear master equation, whose solution can be projected back into a lower-dimensional probability distribution. We will show that the consecutive lifting-projection flow is indeed a nice approximation of the original Boltzmann flow. To address the issue of high-dimensionality, we adopt the tensor train format and compute low-rank solutions with a greedy cross approximation algorithm. Our scheme is consequently faster than the spectral method for the variable hard sphere (VHS) model. Numerical tests are performed to illustrate the efficiency and accuracy.
speaker: Kun Huang

title: Finite Element Methods for Surface Plasmon Polaritons on Complex Graphene Geometries

annotations.one_line_context: This talk details the development of advanced finite element numerical algorithms for simulating surface plasmon polaritons on complex graphene geometries.

abstract: Graphene’s unique electromagnetic properties offer unprecedented control over light at the nanoscale. However, simulating wave propagation on complex graphene sheets requires robust numerical frameworks and rigorous mathematical analysis. Starting from a foundation in Maxwell’s equations, this talk details the development of advanced numerical algorithms tailored for graphene-based surface plasmon polaritons. We will examine the stability and convergence of these methods when applied to complex 2D manifolds. The presentation will conclude with several numerical experiments showcasing the propagation of waves on graphene sheets.
speaker: Li Zhu

title: Towards a Black-Box Laplacian MPS Eigensolver

annotations.one_line_context: This talk presents work on developing a black-box Method of Particular Solutions eigensolver for the Laplacian operator on planar shapes.

abstract: The eigenproblem for the Laplace operator on planar shapes is well-known, and the theory is well understood. However, numerical methods for accurately computing the eigenvalues (and eigenfunctions) of a given planar shape have proven difficult to develop. The Method of Particular Solutions (MPS), which was "revived" by Trefethen and Betcke in 2005, provides the highest accuracy among existing approaches. The drawback is that MPS requires significant shape-specific tuning and basis selection, which limits its direct applicability to problems which require computing the eigenvalues of many different regions (such as in shape optimization or shape inference problems). Here, we present our work on developing a "black-box" MPS eigensolver, which is designed to automatically manage the tuning and basis-selection considerations, enabling its use as the solver within an "inner loop" of a larger problem.
speaker: Hayden Ringer

title: Data-Driven Modal Truncation

annotations.one_line_context: This talk shows how contour integral methods and frequency-domain samples can be used for data-driven modal truncation and model reduction.

abstract: Modal truncation has long been a fundamental approach of model order reduction: to systematically eliminate eigenmodes of a dynamical system that contribute little to the modeling behavior over a given time/frequency range. Typically, this procedure requires the ability to access and utilize intrusive state-space information about the underlying full-order system, which can be infeasible for larger state dimensions or impossible if the full-order system is not known in closed form. Data-driven approaches like proper orthogonal decomposition address these concerns by identifying empirical modes of the system derived from multiple time-domain trajectories of the full-order model, whereafter model reduction can proceed as in the state-space formulation. In this work, we show how one can truncate empirical eigenmodes with only frequency-domain samples of a system's transfer function by utilizing contour integral methods. After reviewing the necessary theoretical foundations, we will discuss how contour integration and the pole-residue decomposition of an underlying system can be combined to identify all eigenvalues within an arbitrary domain in the complex plane. This tool allows us to perform modal truncation, or identify a stable-unstable decomposition of the underlying system. Through the use of a key result of Keldysh, contour integral methods can also identify eigenvalues of analytic nonlinear matrix-valued functions. We will show numerical experiments illustrating how our data-driven modal truncation method performs on application problems and compare with other state-of-the-art methods.
speaker: Dan Folescu

title: CutIGA: a high-order spline-based method for the wave equation

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces a spline-based discretization of the wave equation using the cut finite element method to improve mass matrix conditioning.

abstract: When solving wave problems, it is desirable to use numerical schemes that offer high-order accuracy while maintaining geometric flexibility. One such approach is the cut finite element method (CutFEM), an unfitted method that has primarily been applied to time-independent problems in mechanics, but has also been extended to the wave equation in a series of works by Sticko and Kreiss. However, their approach utilizes a Lagrange basis, which leads to suboptimal conditioning of the mass matrix and a strongly order-dependent CFL condition. In this talk, we provide a brief introduction to CutFEM and present ongoing work on a spline-based discretization of the wave equation in second-order form. We demonstrate a clear improvement in the conditioning of the mass matrix, along with a nearly order-independent CFL condition. We conclude by discussing open questions regarding the existence of optimal stabilization strategies with respect to conditioning.
speaker: Andreas Granath

title: Sketching the Generalized Krylov Subspace Method for Large-Scale Regularized Inverse Problems

annotations.one_line_context: This talk presents sGKS, a sketched variant of the generalized Krylov subspace method that uses randomized dimensionality reduction for large-scale inverse problems.

abstract: The generalized Krylov subspace (GKS) method is an effective projection technique for solving large-scale Tikhonov regularization problems with a general regularization matrix $\Phi$. However, as the subspace expands, the method faces computational bottlenecks from QR factorizations of the tall projected matrices AV k and $\Phi$V k, and from the full reorthogonalization of the basis. In this talk, we present sGKS, a sketched variant that applies randomized dimensionality reduction to each of these bottlenecks. The thin QR factorizations are performed on sketched counterparts of much smaller dimension and maintained incrementally via rank-one updates. Reorthogonalization is carried out in the sketched inner-product space, reducing per-iteration costs while preserving approximation quality as guaranteed by the oblivious subspace embedding property. We provide an analysis showing near-optimality of the sketched projected Tikhonov solution and demonstrate the method on image deblurring, X-ray computerized tomography, and seismic travel-time tomography, where sGKS matches the reconstruction quality of standard GKS at reduced computational cost. This is joint work with Davide Palitta (university of Bologna).
speaker: Mirjeta Pasha

title: Inexactness and Krylov Subspace Regularization

annotations.one_line_context: This talk explores the interplay between inexactness and the regularizing behavior of Krylov subspace methods for inverse problems.

abstract: Linear discrete inverse problems arise in many areas of science and engineering, from medical imaging and geophysics to atmospheric modelling. Their numerical solution often relies on iterative algorithms, particularly Krylov subspace methods, that can efficiently handle large-scale, ill-posed systems. In many practical settings, however, exact computations of matrix–vector products, preconditioners, or right-hand sides are either infeasible or unnecessary, leading to inexact iterations. This talk explores the interplay between inexactness and the regularizing behaviour of Krylov subspace methods for inverse problems.
speaker: Malena Sabaté Landman

title: Priorconditioned Sparsity-Promoting Projection Methods for Deterministic and Bayesian Linear Inverse Problems

annotations.one_line_context: This talk discusses priorconditioned generalized Krylov subspace methods to improve convergence in sparsity-promoting inverse problems.

abstract: High-quality reconstructions of signals and images with sharp edges are needed in a wide range of applications. To overcome the large dimensionality of the parameter space and the complexity of the regularization functional, sparisty-promoting techniques for both deterministic and hierarchical Bayesian regularization rely on solving a sequence of high-dimensional iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) problems on a lower-dimensional subspace. Generalized Krylov subspace (GKS) methods are a particularly potent class of hybrid Krylov schemes that efficiently solve sequences of IRLS problems by projecting large-scale problems into a relatively small subspace and successively enlarging it. We refer to methods that promote sparsity and use GKS as S-GKS. A disadvantage of S-GKS methods is their slow convergence. In this talk, we discuss techniques that improve the convergence of S-GKS methods by combining them with priorconditioning, which we refer to as PS-GKS. Specifically, integrating the PS-GKS method into the IAS algorithm allows us to automatically select the shape/rate parameter of the involved generalized gamma hyper-prior, which is often fine-tuned otherwise. Furthermore, we investigate variations of the proposed PS-GKS method, including restarting and recycling. These respectively leverage restarted and recycled subspaces to overcome situations when memory limitations of storing the basis vectors are a concern. We provide a thorough theoretical analysis showing the benefits of priorconditioning for sparsity-promoting inverse problems. Numerical experiment are used to illustrate that the proposed PS-GKS method and its variants are competitive with or outperform other existing hybrid Krylov methods. This is joint work with Jonathan Lindbloom, Jan Glaubitz, and Youssef Marzouk.
speaker: Mirjeta Pasha

title: Data-driven Balanced Truncation for Mechanical Systems

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces a data-driven second-order balanced truncation method to construct low-dimensional systems with damping structures from frequency domain data.

abstract: Learning dynamical systems from data has emerged as a pivotal area of research, bridging the realms of mathematics, engineering, and data science. Dynamical systems, which describe how states evolve over time based on underlying mathematical relations, are fundamental for understanding a wide range of time-dependent phenomena. For the use of these systems in practical applications like predictive simulations and control, high modeling accuracy as well as interpretability and explainability are essential. All of these desired properties are strongly tied to the internal mathematical structure of the dynamical systems. For example, in the modeling of mechanical or electro-mechanical processes, typically systems with second-order time derivatives. In this case, data are usually given in the frequency domain as samples of the corresponding transfer function. To learn such structured systems from frequency domain data, we develop in this work a data-driven second-order balanced truncation approach. This method allows the construction of low-dimensional second-order systems with generalized proportional damping structure by constructing appropriate Loewner-like matrices. The damping coefficients can be cheaply inferred from given data using gradient-based optimization. Several numerical examples demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
speaker: Steffen Werner

title: The EMAC formulation for fluid models and longer time accuracy

annotations.one_line_context: This talk discusses the energy, linear momentum, and angular momentum conserving (EMAC) scheme and its ability to improve long-time accuracy in fluid and turbulence models.

abstract: This talk will focus on the energy, linear momentum, and angular momentum conserving (EMAC) scheme. We show how EMAC provides improved long-time accuracy for fluid models by leveraging its built-in conservation properties, which mitigate error growth in extended simulations. In addition to standard flow problems, we will discuss its application in the context of Large Eddy Simulation (LES), with particular attention to the Ladyzhenskaya model, and highlight how EMAC can enhance the reliability of turbulence models.
speaker: Jorge Reyes

title: Computation and analysis of unequal counter-rotating vortex pair interactions

annotations.one_line_context: This talk investigates the dynamics and pressure drop mechanisms of unequal counter-rotating vortex pairs using implicit large-eddy simulations.

abstract: The influence of upstream inflow boundary perturbations on the evolution of counter-rotating vortex pairs with unequal strength and size is investigated using implicit large-eddy simulations. Lamb-Oseen vortex pairs are generated at a time-varying inflow boundary condition with parameters based on published experimental work. Previous research efforts have traditionally focused on the stronger (primary) vortex, as it is associated with the lowest average minimum pressure. However, experimental evidence indicate rapid, localized pressure drops in the weaker (secondary) vortex first, motivating the present investigation into the dynamics and mechanisms leading to this phenomenon. Three sinusoidal perturbations are applied to both the primary and secondary vortices at the inflow boundary to determine their effect on long-wavelength instability growth and their subsequent dynamics. The results demonstrate a direct correlation between the initial perturbation amplitude and the streamwise location of the precipitous pressure drop in the secondary vortex. The larger inflow perturbations are shown to accelerate the growth of the Crow instability, leading to accelerated pressure reduction in the secondary vortex closer to the inflow boundary. We seek to quantify the stretching kinematics and evolution along the entire length of the vortex filament, using an adaptive centerline interpolation method informed by the Liutex vector. Furthermore, current investigations look to employ data-driven reduced models to extract the instabilities present in the individual vortex filaments and for simplified and reduced computation.
speaker: Gregory Janes

title: Parameter Estimation for Delay Differential Equations: A New Galerkin Approximation Approach

annotations.one_line_context: This talk presents a Galerkin approximation approach based on orthogonal polynomials to estimate parameters and delays in delay differential equations.

abstract: Delay differential equations with discrete and/or distributed delays are widely used in many applied fields, including mathematical biology, climate science, and engineering. These equations contain free parameters and integral kernels that must be optimized to fit the dynamics of the physical systems they model. We will discuss a method for determining the unknown model parameters, discrete delays, and integral kernels for these equations from data through a Galerkin approximation approach based on a type of orthogonal polynomials due to T. H. Koornwinder. Our approach reduces the problem into the estimation of some scalar parameters in the resulting Galerkin ordinary differential equations. Thanks to the analytical nature of the approximation, this latter estimation problem can be handled efficiently even in the challenging cases of distributed delays. We will provide an overview of the proposed method along with its application to some examples that exhibit chaotic dynamics.
speaker: JC Hartman

title: An Adaptive Low-Rank Method for the Navier Stokes Equations

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces a novel low-rank numerical method for solving the Navier-Stokes equations by dynamically updating the solution rank.

abstract: For many time-dependent problems in fluid dynamics, snapshots of the solution are often well approximated by low rank representations. Such approximations are natural when the dynamics are characterized by coherent structures, but such approximations are also (eventually) valid for chaotic flows owing to the effects of diffusion. The low rank property of these dynamics motivates the use of reduced order models and compression techniques. We present a novel low rank method for approximately solving the Navier Stokes equations that dynamically updates the rank of the solution and never evaluates the solution on the entire grid. The method is based on a pseudo-spectral discretization in space and Runge-Kutta time-stepping. The incompressibility condition is preserved by solving an elliptic problem for which we present a direct low rank solver based on the fast Fourier transform and the CrossDEIM algorithm. The nonlinear terms in the Navier Stokes equations are also approximated with CrossDEIM. Finally, we show the effectiveness of the solver for a few classical test cases.
speaker: Amit Rotem

title: Two-Level Sketching Alternating Anderson acceleration for Complex Physics Applications

annotations.one_line_context: This talk presents a two-level sketching alternating Anderson acceleration method to speed up fixed-point iterations in complex multi-physics PDE simulations.

abstract: We develop a progression of methods for accelerating fixed-point iterations by leveraging approximate and reduced formulations of Anderson acceleration (AA). Firstly, we establish rigorous theoretical error bounds that enable approximate calculations within AA when solving linear problems. We prove that, as long as the approximate computations satisfy these bounds, the convergence guarantees of AA are preserved while computational cost can be reduced. Guided by these results, we introduce computable heuristic quantities that automate accuracy tuning in practice, ensuring monotonic residual reduction and convergence within prescribed tolerances. Motivated by this analysis, we propose a reduced variant of AA in which the least-squares system underlying Anderson mixing is projected onto an adaptively chosen subspace. Secondly, we extend the paradigm to a novel two-level sketching Alternating Anderson–Picard (AAP) method for challenging single- and multi-physics PDE simulations. Our extension combines a static, physics-informed projection (e.g., via Schur-complement reduction to the most informative field) with a dynamic, algebraic sketching stage derived from backward stability analysis under Lipschitz continuity. To balance stability and efficiency, we design inexpensive error estimators and cache-aware randomized sketching strategies that minimize memory footprint and computational overhead. Implemented in Julia, our two-level sketching AAP achieves up to 50% reductions in time-to-solution over standard AA, while maintaining convergence robustness, on benchmark problems including Stokes, p-Laplacian, Bidomain, and Navier–Stokes systems. Together, these contributions provide a rigorous theoretical basis and scalable algorithmic extensions that make Anderson-type accelerations more efficient, adaptive, and applicable across a wide range of scientific computing problems.
speaker: Massimiliano Lupo Pasini

title: Preconditioning techniques for almost symmetric operator equations in Newton-NEPv

annotations.one_line_context: This talk explores direct and iterative preconditioners to accelerate Krylov subspace solvers for correction equations in nonlinear eigenvalue problems.

abstract: This talk aims at presenting different techniques to accelerate the convergence of Krylov subspace solvers for the correction equation in Newton’s method for nonli near eigenvector problems (NEPv). While this operator equation is generally unsym metric, its structure allows a splitting into symmetric and nonsymmetric parts which can be used to derive efficient direct and iterative preconditioners. We will show how to obtain that splitting of the update equation, discuss a selection of preconditioning techniques present in the literature and adapt them to the particular problem. Some numerical comparisons on a discrete Kohn-Sham example complete the talk.
speaker: Tom Werner

title: Atomistic-to-Continuum modeling and Dirac operators in topological materials

annotations.one_line_context: This talk presents a mathematical framework to upscale atomic-level tight-binding models to effective Dirac partial differential equations for topological materials.

abstract: We present a theoretical framework with numerical validation for upscaling atomic-level discrete tight-binding models to effective Dirac partial differential equations governing macroscopic electron propagation in locally periodic topological materials. Applications include the Haldane model, commensurate as well as twisted multi-layer 2D materials such as graphene. We briefly discuss the spectral theory for obtaining multi-band macroscopic models through Taylor expansion of the pseudo-differential operator symbol near band structure degeneracy points. We then propose efficient numerical discretization strategies for the nonstandard effective Dirac equations and confirm theoretical predictions for both bulk states and topological edge states.
speaker: Paul Cazeaux

title: Fast prediction of plasma instabilities with sparse-grid-accelerated optimized dynamic mode decomposition

annotations.one_line_context: This talk shows how sparse grid interpolation accelerates parametric reduced-order models using optimized dynamic mode decomposition for plasma simulations.

abstract: Parametric data-driven reduced-order models (ROMs) that embed dependencies in a large number of input parameters are crucial for enabling many-query tasks in large-scale problems. These tasks, including design optimization, control, and uncertainty quantification, are essential for developing digital twins in real-world applications. However, standard training data generation methods are computationally prohibitive due to the curse of dimensionality, as their cost scales exponentially with the number of inputs. This presentation focuses on efficient training of parametric data-driven ROMs using sparse grid interpolation with Leja points, specifically targeting scenarios with higher-dimensional input parameter spaces. Leja points are nested and exhibit slow growth, resulting in sparse grids with low cardinality in low-to-medium dimensional settings, making them ideal for large-scale, computationally expensive problems. Focusing on gyrokinetic simulations of plasma micro-instabilities in fusion experiments as a representative real-world application, we construct parametric ROMs for the full 5D gyrokinetic distribution function via optimized dynamic mode decomposition (optDMD) and sparse grids based on Leja points. For a real-world electron temperature gradient driven micro-instability simulation featuring six input parameters, we demonstrate that an accurate parametric optDMD ROM can be constructed at a cost of only 28 high-fidelity gyrokinetic simulations thanks to sparse grids.
speaker: Ionut Farcas

title: Towards a reduced order model for hyperbolic partial differential equations

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces a model order reduction technique for parameter-dependent hyperbolic PDEs using a spatially shifted dictionary of solutions.

abstract: In many scientific tasks such as partial differential equation (PDE) constrained optimization, repeated simulation of complex, parameter dependent PDEs is required. Simulation of the PDE for many different parameters is often the dominant cost in these procedures. The goal of model order reduction (MOR) is to produce a reduced order model (ROM) which approximates the PDE solution at a much lower computational cost. MOR is typically accomplished by projecting the PDE dynamics onto a low dimensional linear subspace which well approximates the PDE solution manifold. Hyperbolic PDEs are an important subclass of PDEs which typically arise from modeling conservation laws (i.e., conservation of mass or momentum). Standard MOR techniques are often not effective for producing ROMs of hyperbolic PDEs as their solution manifolds cannot be well approximated by linear subspaces of small dimension. In this talk, we introduce a MOR technique specifically designed for parameter dependent hyperbolic PDEs. Our method first computes an intermediate ROM solution via a finite volume approximation, then constrains the ROM solution to a spatially shifted dictionary of precomputed PDE solutions. The ROM approximation is taken to be the best approximation from the shifted dictionary to the intermediate ROM solution in the L1 norm. Throughout the talk, we use Burgers' equation to motivate and demonstrate our method.
speaker: Mike Ackermann

title: Tensor-Structured Sketching for Very High-Dimensional Problems

annotations.one_line_context: This talk reviews structured random projections and tensor-aware sketches to construct a unified compression framework for high-dimensional multilinear problems.

abstract: Very high-dimensional data with multilinear structure – such as tensors arising from discretized PDEs, quantum chemistry, and multiway feature maps – render standard sketching tools impractical due to infeasible storage and computational requirements. In this talk, we review structured random projections and tensor-aware sketches and introduce a unified framework that fuses separable (Khatri-Rao) projections with tensor train-compatible compression. The resulting sketches are memory-sparse, fast to apply, and come with numerical guarantees of approximate subspace-geometry preservation, along with theoretical results that circumvent exponential scaling in the dimension while incurring minimal and controllable additional error.
speaker: Rodrigo Figueroa Justiniano

title: nlKrylov: A Unified Framework for Nonlinear GCR-type Krylov Subspace Methods

annotations.one_line_context: This talk introduces a unified algorithmic framework generalizing linear GCR-type Krylov solvers to solve systems of nonlinear equations.

abstract: In this talk, we introduce a unified framework for nonlinear Krylov subspace methods (nlKrylov) to solve systems of nonlinear equations. Building on classical GCR-type linear Krylov solvers such as GMRESR, we generalize these approaches to nonlinear problems via nested algorithmic structures. We present rigorous convergence results for problems, relying on relaxed assumptions that avoid the need for exact line searches. Extensive numerical experiments validate the theoretical insights and demonstrate the robustness and efficiency of our proposed algorithms.
speaker: Ning Wan
